drills.q: Trace Microsoft's GenAI platform rebrand history and explain why the November 2025 rename is more than cosmetic.
drills.a: Azure AI Studio (GA May 2024) -> Azure AI Foundry (Nov 2024 Ignite) -> Microsoft Foundry (Nov 2025 Ignite). The 2025 rename drops 'Azure' specifically to signal agents are meant to be first-class across the entire Microsoft ecosystem (365, Copilot, Teams) rather than scoped as just another Azure service -- a positioning shift layered on continuous underlying product evolution.

drills.q: Explain why a workload can hit Azure OpenAI rate limits in one region while having unused quota in another.
drills.a: Azure OpenAI quota (TPM, and RPM derived from it) is enforced per region, per model, per subscription -- not a global pool. A deployment in one region draws only against that region's quota for that model; unused quota elsewhere provides zero relief.

drills.q: A team wants to move a production Azure OpenAI workload to PTU. What do you need before recommending it?
drills.a: Measured sustained monthly token volume compared against the pay-as-you-go break-even (~150-200M tokens/month for GPT-4o-class). PTU bills a fixed hourly rate regardless of consumption (~$1/PTU-hr, ~$260/mo reserved) -- below break-even it's paying for idle capacity.

drills.q: Compare Foundry Agent Service, Bedrock AgentCore, and Vertex AI Agent Builder on their single most differentiating capability each.
drills.a: Foundry Agent Service: first-party GPT-5/OpenAI-frontier access plus deep MS365/Teams integration, unmatched by the others. Bedrock AgentCore: most framework-agnostic, microVM-per-session isolation for ~8hr sessions, episodic memory at GA. Vertex AI Agent Builder: originated the A2A protocol, deepest low-code tooling (ADK 7M+ downloads).

drills.q: As of early 2026, how does Foundry Agent Service's memory feature compare to Bedrock AgentCore's, and why does it matter for design?
drills.a: Foundry's native memory reached public preview only in Q1 2026, while Bedrock AgentCore shipped episodic memory at its October 2025 GA -- a real maturity gap. Any agent design depending on persistent cross-session memory as a core capability needs to build custom memory management on top of Foundry or accept preview-stability risk.

drills.q: Explain why 'hybrid search' on AI Search doesn't automatically guarantee semantic ranking is active.
drills.a: Hybrid search (BM25 + vector fusion) works regardless of tier once vector search is available. Semantic ranking is a separate, optional re-ranking step -- unavailable on Free tier, and requires explicit configuration (a semantic configuration naming fields to rank) even on tiers that support it. A pipeline can run genuine hybrid search while silently missing semantic re-ranking if that step was skipped.

drills.q: A high-concurrency RAG app using AI Search's semantic ranker starts seeing outright request rejections under load. Diagnose.
drills.a: The semantic ranker's internal request queue filled -- once full, further requests are rejected outright rather than gracefully degrading (e.g., silent fallback to non-semantic ranking). Fix: scale replicas/tier to raise the concurrency ceiling, and add an explicit fallback path to non-semantic hybrid search for bursts exceeding capacity.

drills.q: Explain the mechanical difference between an Azure OpenAI 'deployment' and calling OpenAI's own API or Bedrock/Vertex directly.
drills.a: Azure OpenAI requires creating a deployment -- a named binding of a model version to assigned capacity (TPM or PTU) -- and API calls reference the deployment name, not the raw model name. This indirection enables per-deployment capacity assignment and content-filter configuration, letting one resource host multiple differently-configured deployments of the same model.

drills.q: Design the platform choice for an enterprise needing deep Teams integration, GPT-5 access, and a fallback if Foundry's memory preview proves unstable.
drills.a: Foundry Agent Service is the correct choice given the explicit Teams and GPT-5 requirements -- no competitor offers both. For memory risk, design the agent to persist session-relevant facts explicitly to an app-controlled store (Cosmos DB or AI Search) rather than depending solely on Foundry's preview-stage native memory, allowing graceful fallback if it proves unstable.

drills.q: Why does Azure's exclusive first-party GPT-5 access matter architecturally for a cloud-agnostic AI system, not just commercially?
drills.a: A cloud-agnostic abstraction layer can swap between providers offering comparable-tier models, but cannot swap to an equivalent GPT-5 elsewhere since it's Azure/OpenAI-exclusive -- true multi-cloud portability for the frontier model tier doesn't exist today. A sound architecture decision states this lock-in tradeoff explicitly rather than assuming full provider-agnosticism is achievable for free.

drills.q: Explain AI Search's vector index quota model and its planning implication for a growing corpus.
drills.a: Vector quota is a memory constraint scaled per partition (roughly 35GB per partition for post-April-2024 S1 services) -- HNSW-indexed fields must reside fully in memory during queries. A growing vector corpus without partition-count planning hits the memory ceiling before any storage ceiling, since exhaustive KNN (which pages into memory dynamically) is the only vector field type that doesn't consume this quota.
